Court's order requiring 'Comment' rather than outright dismissal

stances.claim: The Court could have legitimately dismissed the ATA petitions at sight on multiple procedural grounds -- prematurity (Section 58 makes the law effective only 15 days after publication), lack of actual controversy, lack of clear legal right, lack of cause of action, lack of locus standi -- as it did in De Leon v. Duterte (May 8, 2020); but it chose not to.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-dismissal-could-have-happened (anchoring institutional choice against available alternative)

stances.claim: By requiring respondents to file Comment instead of dismissing the petitions, the Court has signaled willingness to veer from the analytical school of jurisprudence (Austin-style strict syllogism, dismissal-on-defects) toward the sociological school (Pound-style transcendental-importance doctrine, as in David v. Arroyo) to address ATA's substantive constitutional issues.
stances.rhetorical_move: jurisprudential-school identification (using the analytical/sociological dichotomy as institutional choice frame)

stances.claim: The ATA raises three novel and transcendental issues that need clear resolution: (1) whether terrorism-war emergency can justify executive arrest power that bypasses the constitutional requirement of probable cause personally determined by a judge; (2) whether Congress can modify the Rules of Court on warrantless arrests when the Constitution expressly grants that rule-making power to the Supreme Court; (3) whether the ATA's acts of terrorism are unconstitutionally vague or overbroad.
stances.rhetorical_move: three-issue enumeration (clear-headed framing of the substantive constitutional questions)

stances.claim: The Court has successfully adjudicated novel laws -- cybercrime, money laundering -- that the Framers could not have contemplated, deciding them on the merits with minimal esoteric legalese; ATA deserves the same treatment.
stances.rhetorical_move: precedent-of-novel-adjudication (citing prior practice to anchor expected practice)

stances.claim: The Court should decide the petitions speedily, head-on, on their merit, in clear and simple language -- delivering substantial justice understandable by ordinary citizens, free of legal gobbledygook intelligible only to lawyers.
stances.rhetorical_move: plain-language imperative (institutional virtue framed as accessibility)

notable_anecdotes: CJ's parenthetical tribute embedded in citation: 'David v. Arroyo (May 3, 2006, superbly penned by Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez during my term as CJ)' -- the very citation that Sandoval-Gutierrez emailed CJ about the following week ('I wonder why you keep citing me'), giving this column anecdotal context that resurfaces in C54.

The death-penalty parallel as exemplar of 'actual controversy': only those arrested, investigated, or detained under a death-penalty law can challenge it -- a clean teaching example for distinguishing legal-standing rules.
The historical observation that 'The Constitution and the Rules were composed when terrorism was not yet born' -- making the ATA case a genuine constitutional novelty rather than a routine challenge.
The closing call for 'substantial justice understandable by ordinary citizens, free of legal gobbledygook intelligible only to lawyers' -- one of CJ's most concise democratic-accessibility credos.

The contrasting case De Leon v. Duterte (May 8, 2020) where the Court dismissed at sight a petition to disclose the President's health records -- invoked as the analytical-school move the Court could have but did not deploy here.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban observes that the Supreme Court could have dismissed at sight the many petitions challenging the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020 on familiar procedural grounds -- prematurity (since Section 58 of the ATA itself makes the law effective only 15 days after Official Gazette publication, an inflection date of July 18, 2020), lack of actual controversy, lack of clear legal right, lack of cause of action, lack of locus standi -- as it did just two months earlier in De Leon v. Duterte (May 8, 2020). Instead, the Court ordered respondents to file Comment without yet giving due course, signaling its willingness to veer from John Austin's analytical school of jurisprudence toward the sociological school epitomized by David v. Arroyo (May 3, 2006, 'superbly penned by Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez during my term as CJ') and address transcendental-importance issues on the merits. He frames the ATA case around three novel and transcendental constitutional issues: (1) whether the war on terrorism can justify an innovative reading of the constitutional guarantee that 'no warrant of arrest shall issue except upon probable cause to be determined personally by the judge' vis-à-vis the ATA's Anti-Terrorism Council (composed only of executive officials) authorizing arrest and 24-day detention; (2) whether Congress can amend the Rules of Court on warrantless arrests when the Constitution expressly grants that rule-making power to the Supreme Court; (3) whether the ATA's terrorism acts are unconstitutionally vague or overbroad. Citing the Court's successful adjudication of other novel laws (cybercrime, money laundering) the Framers could not have contemplated, he closes with a 'fervent hope' that the Court will decide the petitions 'speedily, head-on, on their merit, in clear and simple language' -- delivering 'substantial justice understandable by ordinary citizens, free of legal gobbledygook intelligible only to lawyers.'
